text.p: Canberra Watch pointed out last week that if key independent senator Mal Colston were to leave parliament then any delay in replacing him would suit the government.

The observation seems more pertinent today, after Queensland state government statements raised the possibility of some legal confusion over any replacement and after a parliamentary office said it had found apparent irregularities in Colston's expense claims.
Parliamentary officials reported on the weekend that Colston's travel claims appeared to conflict with airline records.
Colston, answering accusations of improper dealings levelled against him last week and earlier, denies any wrongdoing.
But if he were to depart parliament, the Queensland state government has to appoint a replacement.

A quick read of the constitution by this bush lawyer seems to show fairly clearly that Queensland would have to appoint someone from the party with which Colston was identified when elected -- that is, the Labor Party.
The relevant section was amended in 1977 after Labor failed to get Colston himself appointed in 1975 to fill a vacancy.
But Queensland Premier Rob Borbidge said on the weekend he might appoint an independent -- which is what Colston has been since he defected from Labor on budget day in August last year.
Regardless of the rights and wrongs of this, the issue would presumably end up in the High Court, with all the delay that one might imagine.
The delay would please the government.

As noted in this column last week, the government senators would need only 38 votes (which is themselves plus independent Brian Harradine) to win divisions in a Senate that has only 75 members, which it would if Colston were absent but unreplaced.
But let's not run ahead of ourselves. Colston has not been charged, much less convicted, of any offence and he is still not only a senator but also deputy president of the upper house.
So far this is all quite speculative, and its prominence in the media over the past 24 hours is partly explained by the fact that weekends produce little news.
HOWARD'S RESPONSE
Prime Minister John Howard in question time today gave an indeterminate answer to a question about Borbidge's assertion.
The government would abide by the letter and spirit of the constitution, he said.
Abiding by the letter of the law goes without saying but his reference to the "spirit" implies a lack of interest in stretching things.
But then, who is to say what the spirit of the law is?
This part of the issue could all blow over anyway. Borbidge might back down from his assertion.
